references.title: A Taxonomy of Obfuscating Transformations

positions.paragraph:
\subsection{Code watermarking and its evaluation}
Software watermarking predates neural code generation. Early schemes embedded identifiers in control flow, object structure, program state, or source-level transformations, and were evaluated for stealth, robustness, and resistance to semantics-preserving attacks~\cite{collberg1997,venkatesan2001,stern2000,monden2000,collberg2002,nagra2004}. Two lessons from that literature carry over. The transformation is constrained by the behavior the program must preserve, whatever the detector does, and robustness is always relative to a transformation class and attacker model rather than an intrinsic property of a detector score.

positions.paragraph:
\subsection{Code watermarking and its evaluation}
Software watermarking predates neural code generation. Early schemes embedded identifiers in control flow, object structure, program state, or source-level transformations, and were evaluated for stealth, robustness, and resistance to semantics-preserving attacks~\cite{collberg1997,venkatesan2001,stern2000,monden2000,collberg2002,nagra2004}. The transformation is constrained by the behavior the program must preserve, whatever the detector does, and robustness is always relative to a transformation class and attacker model rather than an intrinsic property of a detector score.

positions.paragraph: Existing methods address neighboring parts of this problem. Regression-test selection and prioritization avoid re-executing tests that a change cannot affect~\cite{rothermel1997,yoo2012,rothermel2001}, and active testing chooses informative labels for score estimation~\cite{kossen2021active}. These techniques optimize fault detection or the accuracy of one score; they do not certify the order of two aggregates for every possible value of the labels that remain unknown. Partial identification gives such worst-case guarantees by retaining the set of values compatible with incomplete data~\cite{manski2003}, but applying it separately to each version lets one shared label be valid in one score and invalid in the other. On the MBPP comparison above, separately bounded scores need 811 candidate suites before the order is forced, although the three decisive facts are fixed after one.

\subsection{Test reuse, selection, and active evaluation}
Regression-test selection avoids re-executing tests that a change cannot affect. Safe techniques preserve fault-detection capability under explicit assumptions, and empirical studies characterize their granularity, precision, and cost~\cite{rothermel1997,rothermel1998,engstrom2010,yoo2012}; prioritization reorders tests so that failures appear earlier~\cite{rothermel2001}; and test selection for learned systems chooses inputs by downstream objectives~\cite{ma2021selection}. These lines motivate avoiding redundant suites, but change-based reuse does not answer our identity question: the same candidate can have different labels under different references or harnesses, and rows from different production paths can assert the same proposition. Our stopping objective also differs from preserving every test outcome. An obligation may remain unexecuted because its coefficient is zero in the current comparison, although it still matters to each score.
